extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and writers interested in Norse mythology, hero-worship, and literary/creative criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for depicting Norse-style myth, heroic character, and the cultural process of hero-worship; useful for writers and critics seeking the tone, moral priorities, and symbolic devices characteristic of Norse mythic literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation of the visible workings of Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary characteristic of Norse Mythology is 'Impersonation of the visible workings of Nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nature's forces are depicted as personal agencies (gods, Jotuns): Frost, Fire, Sea-tempest are Jotuns; Summer-heat and the Sun are Gods. Writers should render natural phenomena as miraculous, stupendous, and divine rather than as mere physical processes. Examples: Thor as thunder, Thrym/Rime as hoar-frost driving Hail-Cloud horses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification and agency (gods as natural forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dark hostile Powers of Nature are figured as 'Jotuns' and friendly powers as 'Gods'—the universe divided between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray forces (fire, frost, sea, thunder) with individuality, motives and agency. Use concrete actions and vivid images (e.g., thunder as Thor drawing down his brows; fire-bolt as Thor's hammer) to make nature feel like living characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and earnestness over graceful ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandinavian myth is marked by a 'broad simplicity, rusticity' and 'superior sincerity (far superior) [to] old Grecian grace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value robust, honest, heart-felt depiction rather than elegant/polished prettiness. Tone should be direct, homely, and manlike—less theatrical sublimity, more veracity and strength of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valor as the central moral duty
rubrics_metrics.description: The main practical belief: an inexorable Destiny and that 'the one thing needful for a man was to be brave.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character arcs and cultural values should place subduing fear and personal courage at the core. Bravery is both ethical and existentially decisive—valor determines a man's worth; depict courage as prerequisite to honor and divine favor (e.g., Valkyrs choosing the slain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero as thinker, poet, inventor, and teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Hero embodies intellectual and creative faculties: Odin is portrayed as the original Thinker who invented runes and poetry—'a Poet, Prophet, great devout Thinker and Inventor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct heroic figures whose greatness includes articulate thought and cultural invention (language, poetry, rites). The heroic voice should awaken thought in others; heroes are sources of systems of belief and cultural practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runes and poetry as primal inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Runes (writing) and poetry are presented as monumental inventions—writing as 'the greatest invention man has ever made' and 'a kind of second speech.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In worldbuilding or depiction, treat writing and bardic verse as transformative, quasi-magical technologies that codify and amplify a hero's thought. Use ritualized or signifying texts (runes, songs) as authenticating elements of culture and hero-legends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as layered, historically accretive (Edda as summation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eddas are 'not one coherent System of Thought; but properly the summation of several successive systems.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting or composing myths, account for stratification: multiple eras, voices, and accretions produce inconsistencies and 'confusion.' Expect and use anachronisms, overlapping motifs, and variant versions as signs of authentic oral/collective history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory and poetic delineation are secondary to lived faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegory and poetic symbolism 'cannot be religious Faith; the Faith itself must first be there, then Allegory ... will gather round it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructing myths that are primarily clever allegories without an underlying communal belief or lived practice. Authentic mythic feeling arises from earnest communal attitudes; later poetic elaborations are adjuncts, not substitutes, for the core faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of inexorable Fate (Valkyrs and the Hall of Odin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in an inescapable Destiny—Valkyrs choose the slain, leading the brave to Odin's Hall; base/slavish are thrust elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray cultural outlooks that accept fate as fixed and valorous behavior as the meaningful response. Use ritual and reward frameworks (afterlife for the brave) to motivate heroic action rather than moralizing alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree of Existence (Igdrasil) as organizing metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Igdrasil (the Ash-tree) figures All Life: roots in Death, trunk heaven-high, boughs as histories—'every leaf of it a biography, every fibre there an act or word.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ central, organic metaphors that map cosmic, temporal and moral relations (past/present/future, deeds/lineages). Such a unifying image should convey interconnectedness of actions and history—use it as structural device in narrative or worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust homely humor, pity and directness in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Norse delineations contain 'a heartiness, homeliness, even a tint of good humor and robust mirth' amid fearful things; also 'beautiful traits of pity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance grim or grand events with earthy humor and genuine compassion. Avoid purely grandiloquent or melodramatic treatment; include small humanizing details (e.g., Thor clapping a pot on his head) to make characters relatable and the mythic world believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of heroic culture (valor coupled with productive work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea-roving and battling had social functions—discovering strongest leaders, but many Norse rulers were also 'forest-fellers' and improvers; valor is different from mere ferocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict heroism as socially useful and multifaceted: martial prowess plus productive skills and leadership in settlement or improvement. Avoid romanticizing violence as the sole virtue; show its integration into wider social labor and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradition magnifies the hero (camera-obscura effect of Time)
rubrics_metrics.description: A great man's reputation grows after death—'What mere Time will do ... Tradition! ... a great man ... becomes tenfold greater when dead.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative and critique, allow mythic reputations to diverge from historical fact; use memorialization, place-names, ritual, and linguistic survivals (e.g., 'Wednesday' from Odin) as evidence of cultural magnification. Treat legendary accretions as meaningful even when historically unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic motifs often arise unconsciously (number and pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious symbolic shaping: e.g., the number Twelve 'was enough to determine the Signs of the Zodiac, the number of Odin's Sons'—simple numeric patterns settle into mythic structure unconsciously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurrent symbolic motifs (numbers, cosmological schemas) plausibly and recognizably; accept that some mythic patterns derive from cognitive or cultural predilections rather than deliberate design. These patterns lend cohesion to mythic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish original mythic feeling from later poetic survival
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Eddaic passages are later poetic songs; 'Gray's fragments of Norse Lore ... will give one no notion of it'—later survivals may misrepresent earlier lived belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing or emulating myths, seek the core lived attitudes (sincerity, valor, personification of nature) rather than relying solely on polished surviving fragments. Treat later poetic works as secondary layers that can distort the original cultural temper.
